In this World Cup finals tournament, more than 23% of players—nearly a quarter—were not born in the country they represent, setting a historic high in both proportion and number. Among the 48 participating teams, 8 teams have a majority of players born overseas. Curaçao, a constituent country of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, with a population even smaller than Wan Chai, has only one player on the entire squad who was locally born: Tahith Chong, the team's most marketable player, a Cantonese descendant nurtured by Sheffield United; all the other players come from the Netherlands itself. The stark mismatches in World Cup clashes, apart from giving fans intense viewing experiences, have also put national football associations in a dilemma—they need star players to draw attention, yet also want smaller nations' broadcasters to gain exposure, making it hard to please both sides at once. This tournament has seen constant controversy: fans mock the heavily promoted stars as 'FIFA boys', and representatives of multiple teams have also filed post-match complaints with their federations about the standard of refereeing. For fans, when they look back on the classic matches of the 2026 World Cup years from now, what may be most memorable is perhaps not the final, but the round-of-16 thriller in which defending champions Argentina edged Cape Verde 3-2. Cape Verde's 40-year-old goalkeeper Vozinha (禾舒拿) made a series of saves against Messi's shots, became an overnight sensation, and now has nearly 30 million fans worldwide. On the eve of the previous World Cup, the federation wrote to all participating teams, earnestly asking all sides to 'let football be the protagonist', urging that matches not be drawn into any ideological or political struggles. The World Cup at that time was still hosted by a single country, with 32 national teams participating. The next World Cup will mark the centenary of the tournament, and will unprecedentedly span three continents and be co-hosted by six host nations.
